lede: Before any mechanics question can be answered the forces have to be found and named. A force diagram is that list, drawn: one arrow for every push or pull on the body, each with a label. Get the picture right and the equations almost write themselves.
can: Name every force acting on a body and show it as a labelled arrow
Place weight, normal reaction, tension and friction correctly, on the flat and on a slope
Decide what belongs on a force diagram and what does not, on one body, two joined bodies or a rod

text: A force: a size and a direction

md: Push a book across a table and four forces act on it: the Earth pulls it down, the table pushes it up, your hand pushes it along and the table drags it back.

caption: Four forces on a crate, each an arrow with a label.

md: A force is a vector, with a size and a direction. Each force is drawn as a straight arrow from the body, pointing the way it acts, labelled with its size or its letter. Speeds, accelerations and masses never go on the diagram.

stem: The crate in the picture has a mass of 14 kg. Put the Earth's pull on its force diagram.

steps.working: Mass: 14 kg
steps.decision: A mass is not a force, so it never goes on the diagram as a label.

steps.working: Weight: $14 \times 10 = 140$ N
steps.decision: The Earth's pull on the crate, in newtons, with g = 10 on this paper.

steps.working: An arrow straight down from the crate, labelled 140 N
steps.decision: Drawn from the body, pointing the way the force acts, with its size as the label.

prompt: On the force diagram above, the arrow pointing straight down from the crate is labelled 140 N. Which force is it?
options: the normal reaction on the crate
explain: The Earth pulls the crate down with 140 N, as steps 2 and 3 of See it showed: that is its weight. A mass would be in kilograms, and is not a force at all.

twin.prompt: A book of mass 0.6 kg lies on a desk. Its force diagram has an arrow straight down labelled 6 N. Which force is it?
options: the push of the desk on the book
twin.explain: The Earth's pull on 0.6 kg is 6 N, straight down: the weight. The desk pushes up, not down.

optionNotes.why: A mass is measured in kilograms and is never a force on the diagram.

optionNotes.option: the push of the desk on the book
optionNotes.why: The desk pushes up; the arrow straight down is the Earth's pull.
A mass is in kilograms and is not a force; the arrow's label is in newtons.

optionNotes.option: the normal reaction on the crate
optionNotes.why: The floor pushes up, not down. The downward arrow is the Earth's pull.

md: Drop a body and nothing touches it: the only force on it is its weight, and it falls with acceleration $g$. Newton's second law, $F = ma$, then says the weight is $m \times g$. This paper takes $g = 10$ m/s², so every kilogram weighs 10 newtons.
Mass and weight are easy to mix because everyday speech does: a bag 'weighs 2.5 kilograms'. In mechanics the kilograms are its mass; its weight is always a force, in newtons.

stem: Show that a body of mass m has a weight of mg.

steps.working: Dropped, a body touches nothing: its weight is the only force on it
steps.decision: Nothing else can act, so the weight is the resultant force.

steps.working: It falls with acceleration $g$, so $F = ma$ gives $W = mg$
steps.decision: Newton's second law, with the resultant force being the weight and the acceleration being g.

steps.working: A 2.5 kg bag: $W = 2.5 \times 10 = 25$ N
steps.decision: Its mass stays 2.5 kg; the force it causes is 25 N.

prompt: A sack has a mass of 17 kg. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is its weight, in newtons?
explain: $W = mg$, as in step 3 of See it: $17 \times 10 = 170$ N. The mass is in kilograms; the weight it causes is in newtons.

twin.prompt: A crate has a mass of 27 kg. Taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is its weight, in newtons?

text: Weight points down, even on a slope

alt: A box of mass 18 kg resting on a slope inclined at 20 degrees, with its weight of 180 N drawn straight down from its centre, not down the slope.

caption: Tilt the surface and the weight does not tilt with it.

md: The Earth pulls towards its centre whatever the surface is doing, so the weight arrow is vertical on a floor and still vertical on a slope, drawn from the centre of the body. The 2024 report saw weights that were not drawn vertically.
Later the weight is split into a part down the slope and a part into it. That splitting is working for the equations; on the diagram the weight stays one arrow, straight down.

stem: The box in the picture has a mass of 18 kg and rests on a slope inclined at 20°. Draw its weight.

steps.working: Size: $18 \times 10 = 180$ N
steps.decision: The same weight it would have on a level floor.

steps.working: Direction: straight down, from the centre of the box
steps.decision: The Earth pulls towards its centre, whatever the surface underneath is doing.

steps.working: The slope's 20° changes nothing about the arrow
steps.decision: The angle matters later, when the weight is split; never in the weight's own direction.

prompt: A box of mass 18 kg rests on a slope. A student draws its weight as an arrow of 180 N pointing down the slope, parallel to the surface. What is wrong?
options: The direction: the weight acts vertically downwards
The size: it should be 18 N
Nothing: on a slope the weight acts down the slope
answer: The direction: the weight acts vertically downwards
explain: The size is right, but the Earth pulls straight down whatever the slope, as step 2 of See it showed. The pull down the slope is only a part of the weight, found later; it is not the weight's direction.

twin.prompt: A sack of mass 30 kg lies on a slope. A student labels its weight 30 N and draws it straight down. What is wrong?
options: The size: it should be 300 N
The direction: it should point down the slope
twin.answer: The size: it should be 300 N
twin.explain: The direction is right, straight down, but a weight is the mass times g: 30 × 10 = 300 N.

optionNotes.option: The direction: it should point down the slope
optionNotes.why: The weight points straight down on any surface; the direction was right.
30 is the mass in kilograms; the weight is 300 N.

optionNotes.option: The size: it should be 18 N
optionNotes.why: 18 is the mass in kilograms; the weight is 18 × 10 = 180 N, so the size was right.

optionNotes.option: Nothing: on a slope the weight acts down the slope
optionNotes.why: Only a part of the weight acts down the slope. The weight itself always points straight down.

text: Why the reaction is at right angles

alt: A box on a slope inclined at 30 degrees, with the normal reaction R leaving it at right angles to the slope.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>30°</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M171 128.5L142 78.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M142 78.3L150.6 84.9L143.4 89.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='134' y='80.3' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text></g></svg>
caption: On a slope the reaction R is at right angles to the slope, not to the ground.

md: A surface cannot pull; it can only push back on a body pressing into it. Anything along the surface is friction, a separate force with its own label.

title: Why the push is at right angles
md: The surface pushes only because the body is trying to sink into it, and sinking in is a movement straight into the surface. So the push that stops it comes straight back out, at right angles.

stem: A box rests on a slope inclined at 30°. Find the angle its normal reaction makes with the vertical.

steps.working: The reaction is at $90°$ to the slope
steps.decision: The surface can only push straight back out of itself.

steps.working: With the ground: $90° - 30° = 60°$
steps.decision: The slope is 30° up from the ground, so the reaction leans 60° up from it.

steps.working: With the vertical: $90° - 60° = 30°$, the slope's own angle
steps.decision: Whatever the slope, the reaction leans from the vertical by the slope's angle.

prompt: A box rests on a slope inclined at 40° to the horizontal. What angle does the normal reaction on the box make with the vertical, in degrees?
explain: The reaction is at right angles to the slope, so it makes $90° - 40° = 50°$ with the ground and $90° - 50° = 40°$ with the vertical, as in steps 2 and 3 of See it: the slope's own angle.

twin.prompt: A box rests on a slope inclined at 25° to the horizontal. What angle does the normal reaction on the box make with the vertical, in degrees?
twin.explain: $90° - 25° = 65°$ with the ground, so $90° - 65° = 25°$ with the vertical.

text: Friction: along the surface, against the sliding

alt: A block of mass 4 kg sliding down a rough slope inclined at 30 degrees: R at right angles to the slope, 40 N straight down, friction F up the slope, and a dashed arrow showing the motion down the slope.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='300'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M26 270L366 73.7L366 270Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.07' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M72 270A46 46 0 0 0 65.8 247' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.85'/><text x='80' y='262' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>30°</text><path d='M164.8 189.9L227.2 153.9L202.2 110.5L139.8 146.5Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='183.5' y='145.2' text-anchor='middle' font-size='14' font-weight='600'>4 kg</text><path d='M214.7 132.2L264.9 103.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M264.9 103.2L258.3 111.8L254.1 104.6Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='257.4' y='89.1' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>F</text><path d='M171 128.5L142 78.3' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M142 78.3L150.6 84.9L143.4 89.1Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='134' y='80.3' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>R</text><path d='M183.5 150.2L183.5 228.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M183.5 228.2L179.3 218.2L187.7 218.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='191.5' y='226.2' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>40 N</text><path d='M117.4 123.7L82.8 143.7' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M82.8 143.7l5.9 -9.8M82.8 143.7l11.4 -0.2' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='92.1' y='123.8' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>a</text></g></svg>
caption: The block slides down, so friction F acts up the slope.

md: Friction acts along the surface and against the sliding: a block sliding down a slope has friction pointing up it, and turning the motion round turns friction round. A rough surface gives friction; a smooth one gives none. This paper gives friction as a value or in newtons per kilogram.
A body at rest on a rough slope with nothing attached still has friction: it acts up the slope and holds the body where it is. Take the friction away and the body would slide down.

stem: The 4 kg block in the picture slides down a rough slope, and friction is 2 N for each kilogram of its mass. Draw the friction.

steps.working: The block slides down, so friction acts up the slope, along the surface
steps.decision: Friction opposes the sliding, and it lies along the surface.

steps.working: Size: $2 \times 4 = 8$ N
steps.decision: The rate times the mass, in kilograms.

prompt: A parcel is pushed up a rough slope and is still sliding up it. In which direction does the force due to friction on the parcel act?
options: at right angles to the slope
explain: Friction opposes the sliding, as step 1 of See it showed. This parcel slides up, so friction acts down the slope, along the surface.

twin.prompt: A crate slides east along a rough horizontal floor. In which direction does the force due to friction on the crate act?
twin.explain: The crate slides east, so friction acts west, along the floor, against the sliding.

optionNotes.why: That is the way the crate slides; friction faces the other way.
Vertically up is the floor's normal reaction; friction lies along the floor.
That is the way the parcel is moving; friction acts against the sliding.

optionNotes.option: at right angles to the slope
optionNotes.why: At right angles to the slope is the normal reaction; friction lies along the surface.

stem: The friction on a 30 kg crate is 0.5 N for each kilogram of its mass. Find the friction.

steps.decision: The rate times the mass in kilograms.

steps.working: Not $0.5 \times 300$
steps.decision: Multiplying by the weight, 300 N, gives ten times too much.

prompt: The force due to friction on a crate of mass 22 kg is 1.5 N per kilogram of its mass. What is the force due to friction, in newtons?
explain: The rate times the mass, as step 1 of See it: $1.5 \times 22 = 33$ N. Multiplying by the weight, 220 N, would give ten times too much.

twin.prompt: The force due to friction on a box of mass 14 kg is 2.5 N per kilogram of its mass. What is the force due to friction, in newtons?

text: Tension: a string pulls along itself

alt: A lamp of mass 2.5 kg hanging at rest from a vertical cable: the tension T up along the cable and the weight 25 N straight down.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 290' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='290'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='154' y='123' width='92' height='54' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='200' y='156' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' font-weight='600'>2.5 kg</text><path d='M200 18V123' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><path d='M200 123L200 59' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 59L204.2 69L195.8 69Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='210' y='71' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>T</text><path d='M200 177L200 241' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M200 241L195.8 231L204.2 231Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='210' y='239' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>25 N</text></g></svg>
caption: A cable can only pull, so its tension points up along it.

md: A string, rope or cable can only pull, never push, so its tension acts along the string, away from the body. A body hanging still from one cable has just two forces: its weight down and the tension up, and they balance.
Two strings mean two tensions, with two different letters, because nothing makes them equal. One string over a smooth pulley has a single tension along its whole length.

stem: The lamp in the picture has a mass of 2.5 kg and hangs at rest from a vertical cable. Draw its forces.

steps.working: Weight: $2.5 \times 10 = 25$ N, straight down
steps.decision: The Earth's pull, as always.

steps.working: Tension $T$, up along the cable
steps.decision: A cable can only pull, and it pulls along itself, away from the lamp.

steps.working: At rest, the two balance: $T = 25$ N
steps.decision: Two forces on a still body are equal and opposite.

prompt: A lamp of mass 1.2 kg hangs at rest from a single vertical cable. What is the tension in the cable, in newtons?
explain: Two forces act, as in See it: the weight, $1.2 \times 10 = 12$ N, down, and the tension up along the cable. At rest they balance, so $T = 12$ N.

twin.prompt: A sign of mass 3.4 kg hangs at rest from a single vertical chain. What is the tension in the chain, in newtons?
twin.explain: The weight, $3.4 \times 10 = 34$ N, balances the tension, so $T = 34$ N.

text: Two bodies, two sets of forces

alt: A block of mass 10 kg on a rough table joined by a light string over a smooth pulley at the table's edge to a block of mass 4 kg hanging below. Both parts of the string are labelled T, and friction F acts on the table block, away from the pulley.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 222' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='400' height='222'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><rect x='16' y='92' width='232' height='116' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05'/><path d='M16 92H248V208' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><rect x='78' y='46' width='88' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='122' y='74.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>10 kg</text><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='14' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.8'/><circle cx='268' cy='83' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M268 83L248 104' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><path d='M166 69L268 69' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><path d='M282 83L282 142' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><rect x='254' y='142' width='56' height='46' rx='4' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><text x='282' y='170.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' font-weight='600'>4 kg</text><text x='217' y='61' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>T</text><text x='291' y='120.5' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>T</text><path d='M78 77L32 77' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M32 77L42 72.8L42 81.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='55' y='63' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>F</text></g></svg>
caption: One string, one tension T: the same label at both ends.

md: When two bodies are joined, each gets its own complete set of forces. The block on the table has a reaction and friction; the hanging block has neither, because it touches nothing. A light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension all along, so both ends take the same label $T$.
Draw each body on its own, beside the picture, with only the forces on that body. The string's pull appears twice, once on each body, because it pulls both of them.

stem: The 10 kg block in the picture is on a rough table, joined over a smooth pulley to a 4 kg block hanging below. List the forces on each.

steps.working: The 10 kg block: $10 \times 10 = 100$ N, $R$, $T$ and $F$
steps.decision: It rests on the table, so it has a reaction, and the rough table gives friction.

steps.working: The 4 kg block: $4 \times 10 = 40$ N and $T$
steps.decision: It touches nothing, so it has only its weight and the string's pull.

steps.working: The same letter $T$ at both ends
steps.decision: One light string over a smooth pulley carries one tension.

prompt: Two blocks are joined by a light string passing over a smooth pulley. The tension pulling one block is labelled T. What label should the tension pulling the other block carry?
explain: One string carries one tension, as step 3 of See it showed, so the same letter is used at both ends. A second string would need a second letter.

twin.prompt: Two blocks are joined by a light string over a smooth pulley. The tension at one end is labelled S. What label goes on the tension at the other end?
twin.explain: One string, one tension: the other end is labelled S as well.

text: See it: work round the body

alt: A box of mass 24 kg pulled up a rough slope inclined at 28 degrees by a rope along the slope: T up the slope, F down the slope, R at right angles to the slope and 240 N straight down.

caption: Earth, surface, string, sliding: four forces, four arrows.

stem: A 24 kg box is pulled up a rough slope by a rope along the slope. Find every force on it.

steps.working: Earth: the weight, $24 \times 10 = 240$ N, straight down
steps.decision: Start with the Earth: every body has a weight.

steps.working: Surface: the normal reaction $R$, at right angles to the slope
steps.decision: One contact gives one reaction.

steps.working: String: the tension $T$, up the slope along the rope
steps.decision: The rope pulls along itself, away from the box.

steps.working: Sliding: the box moves up, so friction $F$ acts down the slope
steps.decision: Friction faces the sliding, along the surface.

title: Force diagrams
why: The same four forces put on several bodies in turn. Watch how each arrow is drawn from the body and labelled before any arithmetic starts.

prompt: A crate is pulled up a rough slope by a rope parallel to the slope. How many forces act on the crate?
explain: Work round it as See it did: the Earth gives the weight, the surface the normal reaction, the rope the tension and the sliding the friction, down the slope. Four forces, four arrows.

twin.prompt: A box slides down a smooth slope with nothing attached to it. How many forces act on the box?
twin.explain: Only the weight and the normal reaction: no string, and a smooth slope gives no friction.

title: On the diagram, and never on it
md:
**On:** the weight in newtons, one reaction per contact, one tension per string, friction on a rough surface.
**Never:** a mass in kilograms, a second reaction on one surface, a part of the weight drawn again, a velocity or an acceleration.

title: What the reports keep saying
md: About half the entry misses one of the two diagram marks: a reaction left off, friction the wrong way round, or a force that was never there.
A velocity or an acceleration is not a force either: it describes the motion the forces produce. A dashed arrow for the acceleration may sit beside the diagram, never among the forces.

stem: A box of weight 60 N rests on a rough slope inclined at 30°. A student wants to add the pull down the slope as a fifth arrow. Is it a force?

steps.working: The weight, 60 N, straight down, is already drawn
steps.decision: The Earth gives exactly one force.

steps.working: $60\sin 30° = 30$ N of it acts down the slope
steps.decision: Splitting the weight is working, done later when resolving.

steps.working: Those 30 N are inside the 60 N arrow already
steps.decision: Drawing them as well would count the same pull twice.

prompt: A box rests on a rough slope. Which one of these should not be drawn as a force on the box?
options: the component of the weight down the slope
answer: the component of the weight down the slope
explain: That component is part of the weight, as step 3 of See it showed, and the weight is already on the diagram. Drawing it as well counts the same pull twice.

twin.prompt: A crate is pulled along a rough floor by a rope at an angle. Which one of these should not be drawn as a force on the crate?
options: the vertical part of the rope's pull
twin.answer: the vertical part of the rope's pull
twin.explain: The vertical part is inside the tension arrow already; drawing it again counts the pull twice.

optionNotes.why: The rope pulls the crate, so its tension is a real force on the diagram.
A rough floor gives friction, so it belongs on the diagram.
The slope pushes on the box, so the reaction belongs on the diagram; leaving it off is the commonest slip.
A rough slope gives friction, so it belongs on the diagram.

md: **The other forces** (2019, 2021, 2022). Part of the diagram is printed, usually the pull. Mark only the forces that are missing, and do not draw the printed one again.
**Smooth or rough** (2019 to 2025). The word decides whether friction is drawn at all. **Two blocks** (2022, 2023, 2025): each gets its own set, and the hanging one has only its weight and $T$.
**No extra arrows** (2025). The report penalised arrows that are not forces: a second reaction, a component drawn again, a velocity. Every arrow must be a push or a pull from something.
**Now** (2024). The motion changes, say a box sliding up a slope stops and slides back down, and the part asks for the forces now.

stem: A 1.5 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is pulled by a string, and the pull is already printed on the diagram. Add the missing forces.

steps.working: The weight: $1.5 \times 10 = 15$ N, straight down
steps.decision: The Earth's pull is always missing until you draw it.

steps.working: The normal reaction $R$, straight up
steps.decision: The table pushes back on the block resting on it.

steps.working: No friction, and the pull is not drawn again
steps.decision: Smooth means no friction; the printed pull is already there.

prompt: A block on a smooth horizontal table is pulled by a string, and the pull is already printed on the diagram. Which forces do you add?
options: the weight and the normal reaction
the weight, the normal reaction and friction
the weight, the normal reaction and the pull again
answer: the weight and the normal reaction
explain: The table is smooth, so there is no friction, and the pull is printed already, as step 3 of See it said: only the weight and the normal reaction are missing.

stem: A 3.5 kg box slides up a rough slope, stops, and slides back down. Which arrows change?

steps.working: The weight stays: $3.5 \times 10 = 35$ N, straight down
steps.decision: The Earth's pull does not care which way the box moves.

steps.working: The reaction stays: $R$, at right angles to the slope
steps.decision: One contact, one reaction, whatever the motion.

steps.working: Friction turns round: down the slope while it rises, up the slope as it slides back
steps.decision: Friction always faces the sliding.

prompt: A box slides up a rough slope, stops, and slides back down. Which arrow on its force diagram changes?
explain: Friction always opposes the sliding, so it turns round when the motion does, as step 3 of See it showed; the weight and the reaction stay exactly as they were.

twin.prompt: A crate on a rough floor is pulled east by a horizontal rope, then the rope pulls it west. Which arrows turn round?
options: the tension, the friction and the weight
twin.explain: The rope now pulls west, and the crate slides west, so friction turns to face east: two arrows turn, and the weight and the reaction stay.

optionNotes.why: The rope itself now pulls the other way, so its tension arrow turns round as well.

optionNotes.option: the tension, the friction and the weight
optionNotes.why: The weight points straight down whichever way the crate moves.
The Earth pulls straight down whichever way the box moves.
One contact gives one reaction at right angles to the slope, whatever the motion.

md: Every Summer paper since 2019 asks for all the forces on a rod. A uniform rod's weight acts at its midpoint; each support pushes up with its own reaction; each string pulls with its own tension, two strings taking two letters. The 2019 report saw the weight placed halfway between the strings.
Each support touching the rod gives one reaction, and each string one tension. A load hanging from the rod pulls down on it with the load's weight, at the point where it hangs.

stem: The uniform rod in the picture has a mass of 32 kg and a length of 4 m, with a 50 N load at A, a support at C and a string at B. List its forces.

steps.working: Its weight: $32 \times 10 = 320$ N, at its midpoint M
steps.decision: A uniform rod's weight acts at its middle.

steps.working: M is $4 \div 2 = 2$ m from A
steps.decision: Half the length, measured from either end.

steps.working: With it: the 50 N load, $R$ at C and $T$ at B
steps.decision: One force for the load, one for each support or string.

prompt: A uniform rod hangs horizontally from two vertical strings, and a block hangs from one end of it. How many forces act on the rod?
explain: Count as See it did: its own weight at the midpoint, one tension for each string (two letters), and the pull of the block's string at the end. Four forces.

twin.prompt: A uniform plank rests on two supports with nothing else on it. How many forces act on the plank?
twin.explain: Its weight at the midpoint and one reaction at each support: three forces.

md:
Draw every force as a labelled arrow, the weight as mg in newtons.
Place the weight vertically and the reaction at right angles to the surface.
Turn friction against the sliding, and give one string one tension label.
Give each body of a joined pair, and a rod, its own complete set of forces.
Leave off masses, components and anything that is not a push or a pull.

The opening part of a mechanics question asks you to show every force on the body, on a diagram already printed for you, and it carries two marks: one for roughly half the forces, one for the rest. The first mark is for arrows pointing the right way with labels; the last is for having them all and nothing extra. Stuck? Work round the body: Earth, surface, string, sliding.
